To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the levels of some trace elements, such as Se and Pb, are significantly different between ALS patients and controls, and the levels of Se are significantly different among the ALS patients, according to disease severity.
the levels of Se in blood are significantly higher in ALS patients than in healthy controls, while Pb is significantly lower in ALS patients than healthy controls.

the levels of Selenium in plasma and hair of ALS are lower than those of controls; the levels of Lead in blood of ALS patients are higher than those of controls, and the levels of Lead are higher in the group of ALS patients more affected by the disease than in the group with a lower degree of severity.

the study of the possible role of metals, in particular heavy metals, in the etiology of ALS.
the possible involvement of heavy metals in ALS pathogenesis.
the study of trace elements, in ALS patients and controls, and the possible relationships with the clinical severity of the disease.

the levels of the trace elements in ALS are not easy to be interpreted, but it is possible that some trace elements, such as Selenium, may play an important protective role in the pathophysiology of ALS.
, at the moment, we can only say that a possible role of heavy metal in ALS pathogenesis is not excluded.
the trace elements in the ALS patients do not have a direct involvement in the etiology of this disease, but may be a consequence of the damage caused by the disease itself.

the levels of Selenium in plasma and urine, and the Lead in plasma, could be considered as possible risk factors for ALS.
the levels of metals are not directly involved in the disease, but the presence of metals in the blood may be a marker of the disease severity, because of a change in the metabolism. In
